title: The Lost Art of Being Alone With Your Thoughts

reels.hook: Could you sit alone for 15 minutes with no phone?
reels.hook_b: Most people haven't sat alone with their thoughts since childhood.
cards: Could you sit alone for 15 minutes with no phone?
In one study, many people chose an electric shock instead.
They'd said beforehand they'd pay to avoid it.
We're not broken. We're out of practice.

source.author: Wilson et al.
source.work: Just think: The challenges of the disengaged mind (Science 345)

reels.caption:
In a 2014 study, people sat alone in a room for 15 minutes with nothing to do but think, and a button that gave them a mild electric shock they'd earlier said they would pay to avoid. 67% of men and 25% of women pressed it at least once.

The lesson isn't that thinking is unbearable. It's that most of us are out of practice.

When did you last sit with your own thoughts?

Evidence: Wilson et al. (2014). Full essay on the Substack, link in bio.
reels.first_comment: Honestly: when did you last spend 15 minutes awake with nothing to fill them?

reels.hook: The queue has a phone in it. The walk has a podcast.
reels.hook_b: What 15 minutes of chosen solitude actually does to your mood.
cards: The queue has a phone in it. The walk has a podcast.
The bath has a screen balanced on the edge.
Researchers had people sit alone for 15 minutes, no devices.
Strong feelings dropped. Calm rose. More so when they chose what to think about.
Solitude doesn't make you happier. It turns the volume down.
Send it to someone who never stops.

reels.evidence: Tier 1 studies (N58, details verified via BPS Research Digest); format D, no advice
reels.caption:
Fifteen minutes alone, no phone, no task. Students who did it felt fewer strong emotions afterwards, good and bad, and more calm. The effect was bigger when they chose what to think about. In a diary study, a daily 15 minutes made days less agitated.

Solitude isn't loneliness. It's a short gap in the noise.

Where's your 15 minutes going to be?

Evidence: Nguyen, Ryan & Deci (2018). Full essay on the Substack, link in bio.

carousel_caption:
In one study, many people preferred an electric shock to 15 minutes alone with their thoughts. In another, the same 15 minutes, chosen and device-free, settled strong emotions and raised calm.

The difference seems to be practice, and choosing where to point your mind.

Where will you sit for 15 minutes this week?

Evidence: Wilson et al. 2014; Killingsworth & Gilbert 2010; Nguyen, Ryan & Deci 2018. Philosophy: Pascal, Pensées 139 (Trotter).
notes: People in a 2014 study were left alone with their thoughts for 15 minutes and a button that gave a mild shock. Most men pressed it. The headline was 'people would rather be shocked than think'. The better reading: given no direction, many of us don't know what to do with our own minds. That's practice, not fate.

Pascal, in the 1600s: all of human unhappiness comes from not being able to sit quietly in a room. He wrote that without a phone in sight. Restlessness isn't a smartphone invention. The phone is just the most efficient way we've found to feed it.
One finding worth knowing: in studies of 15-minute device-free solitude, people who chose what to think about got more of the calming effect. Not emptying your mind. Pointing it somewhere.
